# [TASK] Implement User Service

## Task

Implement User Service with JWT authentication, Spring Security, user registration/login, profile management, and favorites/watchlist functionality.

> **Audited 2026-07-22.** This issue was closed with every checklist/acceptance box unchecked. The implementation was verified line-by-line against the code (`backend/user-service`) and live-tested (register → login → profile → favorites/watchlist → refresh → logout, plus a JaCoCo coverage run). Boxes below now reflect reality; the "Domain Model" / "Security Configuration" / "Database Schema" snippets were rewritten to match what was actually built — the originals were the pre-implementation sketch and had drifted. See **Implementation Notes** for the deltas worth knowing about.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] User registration and login working — verified live end-to-end
- [x] JWT access tokens + rotating refresh tokens generated and validated — access tokens validated both locally and via the gateway's shared-secret contract
- [x] Profile management functional — get/update profile, change password, favorites/watchlist add/remove/list (idempotent), all verified live
- [x] Database migrations, Eureka registration, and OpenAPI docs all working — Flyway `V1` applies cleanly, service registers with Eureka, swagger-ui live
- [x] All tests passing at 85%+ coverage — 21/21 tests green; JaCoCo 87% instruction / 88% line / 86% method; TestContainers integration suite covers the full register→login→favorites→refresh→logout journey

**Hours:** 10-12

## API Endpoints

All 13 endpoints below are implemented exactly as specified — verified by direct comparison against `AuthController`/`UserController` and live `curl` testing.

```
POST /api/v1/auth/register          # User registration
POST /api/v1/auth/login             # User login
POST /api/v1/auth/refresh           # Refresh JWT token
POST /api/v1/auth/logout            # User logout
GET  /api/v1/users/profile          # Get user profile
PUT  /api/v1/users/profile          # Update profile
PUT  /api/v1/users/password         # Change password
GET  /api/v1/users/favorites        # Get favorite movies
POST /api/v1/users/favorites/{id}   # Add to favorites
DELETE /api/v1/users/favorites/{id} # Remove from favorites
GET  /api/v1/users/watchlist        # Get watchlist
POST /api/v1/users/watchlist/{id}   # Add to watchlist
DELETE /api/v1/users/watchlist/{id} # Remove from watchlist
```

## Domain Model (as actually implemented)

`Role` is an enum (`USER`, `ADMIN`), not a JPA entity — RBAC only needs a fixed, small set of role names, and an enum avoids an unnecessary join. `Favorite` and `WatchlistItem` are structurally identical but kept as separate tables/entities since their lifecycles are expected to diverge (e.g. future watchlist ordering or watched-state). A `RefreshToken` entity was added beyond the original sketch — see **Implementation Notes**.

```java
@Entity
@Table(name = "users")
@Getter @Setter @Builder @NoArgsConstructor @AllArgsConstructor
public class User {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.UUID)
    private UUID id;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 50)
    private String username;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 255)
    private String email;

    @Column(name = "password_hash", nullable = false, length = 100)
    private String passwordHash;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 20)
    private Role role;               // enum: USER, ADMIN

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private boolean enabled;

    @Column(name = "account_non_locked", nullable = false)
    private boolean accountNonLocked;

    @Column(name = "created_at", nullable = false)
    private LocalDateTime createdAt;

    @Column(name = "last_login")
    private LocalDateTime lastLogin;
}

@Entity
@Table(name = "favorites", uniqueConstraints = @UniqueConstraint(columnNames = {"user_id", "movie_id"}))
public class Favorite {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "user_id", nullable = false)
    private User user;
    @Column(name = "movie_id", nullable = false)
    private Long movieId;            // TMDB id only — movie data lives in movie-service (ADR-002)
    @Column(name = "added_at", nullable = false)
    private LocalDateTime addedAt;
}
// WatchlistItem is structurally identical to Favorite, table "watchlist_items"

@Entity
@Table(name = "refresh_tokens")
public class RefreshToken {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "user_id", nullable = false)
    private User user;
    @Column(name = "token_hash", nullable = false, unique = true, length = 64)
    private String tokenHash;        // SHA-256 hex of the opaque token — raw value never stored
    @Column(name = "expires_at", nullable = false)
    private LocalDateTime expiresAt;
    @Column(name = "created_at", nullable = false)
    private LocalDateTime createdAt;
}
```

## Security Configuration (as actually implemented)

No `UserDetailsService`/`AuthenticationManager` pipeline — login is a direct, custom check in `AuthService` (lookup by username, BCrypt match, `enabled`/`accountNonLocked` checks), and every *subsequent* request is authenticated purely by the stateless `JwtAuthenticationFilter`. This is simpler than a full Spring Security `AuthenticationProvider` setup and sufficient for a stateless-JWT design.

```java
@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
@EnableMethodSecurity   // active for future @PreAuthorize use; nothing uses it yet
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class SecurityConfig {

    private final JwtAuthenticationFilter jwtAuthenticationFilter;

    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .sessionManagement(session -> session.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/api/v1/auth/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/swagger-ui/**", "/swagger-ui.html", "/v3/api-docs/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/hello").permitAll()
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .exceptionHandling(ex -> ex.authenticationEntryPoint(new HttpStatusEntryPoint(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED)))
            .addFilterBefore(jwtAuthenticationFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class);
        return http.build();
    }

    @Bean
    public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
        return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12);   // strength 12, per the security checklist
    }
}
```

`JwtTokenProvider` issues HS256 access tokens with claims `sub` (username), `userId` (account UUID), `roles` (list) — **this exact claim shape is a contract with the API gateway's `JwtUtil`**, which validates with the same shared `jwt.secret`. Changing claim names requires updating both sides.

## Database Schema (as actually implemented — Flyway `V1__init_user_schema.sql`)

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
    id                  UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    username            VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL,
    email               VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    password_hash       VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    role                VARCHAR(20)  NOT NULL,
    enabled             BOOLEAN      NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
    account_non_locked  BOOLEAN      NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
    created_at          TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    last_login          TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT uq_users_username UNIQUE (username),
    CONSTRAINT uq_users_email    UNIQUE (email)
);

CREATE TABLE favorites (
    id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id   UUID      NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    movie_id  BIGINT    NOT NULL,
    added_at  TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT uq_favorites_user_movie UNIQUE (user_id, movie_id)
);

CREATE TABLE watchlist_items (      -- named watchlist_items, not "watchlist"
    id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id   UUID      NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    movie_id  BIGINT    NOT NULL,
    added_at  TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT uq_watchlist_user_movie UNIQUE (user_id, movie_id)
);

CREATE TABLE refresh_tokens (       -- not in the original sketch at all
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id     UUID        NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    token_hash  VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    expires_at  TIMESTAMP   NOT NULL,
    created_at  TIMESTAMP   NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT uq_refresh_tokens_hash UNIQUE (token_hash)
);

-- List queries are always per-user, newest first.
CREATE INDEX idx_favorites_user      ON favorites (user_id, added_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_watchlist_user      ON watchlist_items (user_id, added_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_refresh_tokens_user ON refresh_tokens (user_id);
```

## Implementation Notes (added 2026-07-22 audit)

- **Refresh token rotation, not in the original spec:** refresh tokens are opaque random values, stored only as a SHA-256 hash (a DB leak doesn't leak usable tokens). Every use rotates the token (old row deleted, new one issued) and `logout` deletes all of a user's refresh-token rows — the actual mechanism that makes logout meaningful in an otherwise-stateless JWT system (short-lived access tokens can't be renewed after logout, even though they remain valid until natural expiry — a documented, deliberate trade-off).
- **HATEOAS**, added in a later session (unrelated to this issue's original scope): `GET /api/v1/users/profile` returns a HAL-style resource with `_links` to `self`/`favorites`/`watchlist`.
- **Favorites/watchlist writes are idempotent**: adding an already-favorited movie, or removing one that isn't favorited, both succeed silently rather than erroring — backed by the DB unique constraint plus service-layer handling.
- **user-service has zero TMDB coupling** — it only ever stores/returns bare TMDB movie *ids* for favorites/watchlist; it never calls TMDB or stores movie data (that's movie-service's job, database-per-service per ADR-002).
- **Not yet wired to the real frontend**: the actual React app (a sibling repo, `~/Desktop/filmpire`) currently authenticates against TMDB's own session system, not this service. Retargeting it to user-service's JWT flow is unstarted, tracked as a follow-up to #33/#34.
- **RBAC is infrastructure-only:** JWT `roles` claim → Spring Security authorities, `@EnableMethodSecurity` active — but no endpoint restricts by role yet since there's no admin-only functionality to gate. (Was listed as its own Acceptance Criteria item before this reshape; demoted here since it isn't a cleanly done/not-done milestone the way the other five are.)
